description: I am B V Sai Rakshan and studying Grade 5 in Nehru International School. I am very much interested in space and space related research
summary:
The Quiet Ones is a short story told by Sai Rakshan, a 10-year-old who inherits his grandpa's old radio station. One night it picks up voices from NASA's retired machines, and he starts writing them down as postcards. Each machine tells him why it was sent, what it found out, and where it is now.
The story covers Opportunity, Spirit, Viking 1, Sojourner, Ingenuity, the Apollo landing sites, Surveyor 3, Voyager and Pioneer 10. Instead of listing facts, it lets kids hear them from another kid. For example, Opportunity was built to last 90 days and kept going for almost 15 years. Its little hematite "blueberries" showed that Mars once had water, which is why Perseverance is now looking for signs of ancient life.
Most space stories are about what's launching next. We wanted to show that finished missions still matter, because every old machine left a question behind that newer missions like Perseverance and Artemis are still answering. The machines' voices are made up, but every date, distance and discovery is real.
details:
What it does and how it works

The Quiet Ones is a short story told by Sai Rakshan, a 10-year-old who inherits his grandpa's old radio station. Every so often the radio picks up a "postcard" from a retired NASA machine. Each postcard answers the same three questions: Why was I sent? What did I find out? Where am I now?

The story covers ten sets of hardware on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space: Opportunity, Spirit, Viking 1, Sojourner, Ingenuity, the Apollo 11 landing site, the Apollo rovers, Surveyor 3, Voyager 1 and 2, and Pioneer 10. Instead of reading a list of facts, kids hear them from another kid who is just as surprised by them as they are. By the end, Sai works out that none of the machines are really gone, because newer missions like Perseverance and Artemis are still answering the questions the old ones left behind.

Benefits

•       Kids learn real mission facts without it feeling like homework.

•       It's short, about three pages, so it's easy to read in one sitting or read aloud in class.

•       It connects old missions to new ones, so students see space exploration as one long story.

•       A "what's real and what's made up" section at the end helps kids tell facts from imagination.

Intended impact

We want kids to feel a bit attached to these machines, the way you feel about a toy that's been through a lot. Most children only hear about missions that are launching now. We hope this story shows them that a mission doesn't end when the signal stops, and that it makes them curious enough to go look up Perseverance, Artemis and the Voyagers on their own. Teachers could also use it as a reading activity that happens to teach some science.

Tools and software

•       Claude, an AI assistant, helped us brainstorm the idea, outline it and write early drafts. We then rewrote the story in a child's voice and simplified the language.

•       Microsoft Word for the final story and these project documents.

•       Facts are based on NASA's published mission histories.

No coding or special hardware was needed for this version. An interactive web version (HTML, CSS and JavaScript) with a clickable map of the Moon and Mars is an idea for a next step.

What makes it creative

•       The narrator is a child, so the science sounds like something a friend would tell you, not a textbook.

•       The postcard idea gives every machine its own little voice and the same simple structure, which makes them easy to remember.

•       The story turns real details into emotional moments. Spirit got stuck in sand and kept working anyway. Opportunity was built for 90 days and lasted almost 15 years. Ingenuity was planned for about five flights and flew 72.

•       It's honest about what's imagined. The voices are made up, but the facts are real, and the story says so.

What we considered

•       Age: we aimed at ages 9 to 14, with short sentences and simple words.

•       Accuracy: we corrected small details that often get repeated wrongly. For example, Opportunity's famous "my battery is low and it's getting dark" line was a reporter's way of explaining the data, and the story says that. Spirit got stuck in 2009, not 2010.

•       Facts that change: Voyager's distance grows every day, so the story says "almost a whole day" for its signal time instead of an exact number.

•       Tone: the machines are curious and a little funny, not dramatic or sad, so kids come away inspired.

•       Credit: any NASA pictures added later should follow NASA's media usage guidelines.
